newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai to push state firm bankruptcies in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai to push state firm bankruptcies in 1997.

text.p: Shanghai will encourage more state firms to go bankrupt this year while trying to improve the system to cope with the expected new flood of laid-off workers, local officials said on Monday.

Some 58 companies went bankrupt in Shanghai last year and the number of bankruptcies will rise significantly in 1997, said Xu Jianguo, deputy director of the Shanghai Economic Commission. He declined to give an estimate of this year's number.
"Bankruptcies are a normal thing in a market economy," he told reporters at a briefing. "We expect bankruptcies to increase as we try to solve the problems from the last 40 years."
The legacy of China's state enterprise system is widespread inefficiency, high levels of indebtedness and over-manning in most state-run companies, he said.
"The government wants to increase bankruptcies, but at the same time we are very careful in implementing the policies," Xu said.
Encouraging bankruptcies is a sensitive social issue requiring careful handling of the workers thrown out of work in the process, officials say.
"We are facing a real difficulty in the future with laid off workers," said Ye Mingzhong, deputy director of the Shanghai Municipal Labour Bureau.

State enterprises in Shanghai laid off 230,000 workers in 1996 alone, bringing the total number to around one million since the painful process of restructuring the state firms began in the early 1990s, he told reporters.
The city found jobs for around the same number of laid-off workers during 1996, keeping the overall unemployment rate for the city stable, according to officials.
Ye said Shanghai's unemployment rate was 2.8 percent at the end of 1996 and the city aims to control the rate at between three and four percent in the future.
The city in 1996 started a pilot programme with re-employment centres to provide vocational training and help workers find new jobs, he said.
